chapters.name: Chapter 1: Reading closely and writing correctly

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How the GED language arts test works
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the parts of the GED language arts test and write a study plan with dates.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official GED website, you will list the parts, question types and time of the GED language arts test and write a study plan with dates, with every part of the test named and at least one study date each week until the test.
The GED has four tests: Math, Reasoning Through Language Arts (RLA), Science and Social Studies. You can take them one at a time. The GED Testing Service makes the test. Some states use another high school equivalency test, HiSET, so check which test your state uses.
On ged.com, the RLA test is listed as 150 minutes in three sections, with a 10-minute break between parts 2 and 3. It covers reading for meaning, finding and making arguments, and grammar and language. One section is a written essay, called the extended response, with 45 minutes.
Most questions are multiple choice. Others ask you to drag and drop, select an area of the screen, or pick from a drop-down list in a sentence. Ged.com lists a passing score of 145 for each subject. Times and rules can change, so check ged.com before you book.
A plan beats cramming. Short practice four or five days a week works better than one long night. Ged.com has free sample tests and an official practice test, GED Ready, which shows if you are likely to pass.
Step by step:
- Go to ged.com and read the Reasoning Through Language Arts page.
- Write down the time, the sections and the question types.
- Take the free sample RLA test to see where you stand.
- Pick a target test week and count the weeks until then.
- Write at least one study date each week, with the lesson or skill for that day.
Words to know:
- GED: a high school equivalency test; passing all four subjects earns a credential that many employers and colleges accept like a diploma.
- HiSET: another high school equivalency test that some states use.
- Extended response: the GED word for the essay you write on the test.
- Drop-down: a list that opens when you click it, so you can pick one answer.
- Study plan: a calendar of what you will practice and when.
Official sources:
- GED Testing Service: test subjects (time, question types, essay)
- GED Testing Service: scores
- GED Testing Service: free sample tests (English and Spanish)
- GED Ready, the official practice test
- HiSET, another high school equivalency test (official site)
Try it now: Open ged.com and take the free RLA sample test (or read the RLA page if you cannot take it now). Then write your study plan: your target test week, and one date each week with the skill you will practice (reading, grammar, arguments or the essay). Keep it; you will add to it.
You can now name the parts of the GED language arts test and follow a study plan with dates.

check.q: What is the extended response on the GED language arts test?
options: The essay you write on the test
check.why: Ged.com calls the written essay the extended response.

check.q: Your test is 8 weeks away. Which plan is best?
options: Study 30 minutes on four days each week, with a skill for each day
Study all night the day before
Take the test with no practice to see what happens
check.why: Short, regular practice with a planned skill each day builds skills better than cramming.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Main idea, details and inferences
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the main idea, two supporting details and one inference in a short passage.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short passage, you will identify the main idea, the supporting details and an inference backed by evidence, pointing to the exact sentence that supports each answer.
The main idea is what the whole passage is mostly about. Supporting details are the facts, examples and reasons that back it up. Ask: "If I had to say this passage in one sentence, what would I say?"
Worked example. Passage: "Many warehouses now run all night. Night shifts often pay more per hour. But workers on night shifts report more trouble sleeping, and some say it is harder to see their families." Main idea: night shifts pay more but have costs for workers. Details: they pay more; workers report sleep trouble; family time is harder.
An inference is a smart guess based on clues in the text. It is not written word for word, but the text supports it. From the passage, you can infer that a worker with young children might think twice about a night shift. You cannot infer that night shifts are against the law; nothing says that.
On the test, always point to the sentence that proves your answer. If you cannot point to it, the answer is probably wrong.
Step by step:
- Read the question first, so you know what to look for.
- Read the passage once all the way through.
- Say the main idea in one sentence.
- Find two details that support it.
- For an inference, pick the answer the text supports, and find the sentence that proves it.
Words to know:
- Main idea: what a passage is mostly about.
- Supporting detail: a fact, example or reason that backs up the main idea.
- Inference: a conclusion you reach from clues in the text.
- Evidence: the words in the text that prove an answer.
Try it now: Practice passage: "The city opened three new cooling centers this summer. On days over 100 degrees, they stayed open until 10 pm. Visits were highest among older adults and people without air conditioning." 1) Main idea? 2) Two details? 3) Which inference is supported: (a) the city wants to protect people from heat, or (b) the centers cost too much? Answers: 1) The city opened cooling centers to help people in hot weather. 2) Open until 10 pm on very hot days; most visitors were older adults and people without air conditioning. 3) (a). Nothing in the passage talks about cost.
You can now find the main idea, the details and a supported inference, and point to the proof.

check.q: A passage says a bakery added an evening shift, hired five people and sold 30% more bread. What is the main idea?
options: Adding an evening shift helped the bakery grow
check.why: The whole passage is about the evening shift helping the bakery; the hires and sales are details.

check.q: Which is an inference, not a detail written in the text?
options: A fact copied word for word from the passage
A conclusion you reach from clues the text gives
check.why: An inference is a conclusion supported by clues, not a fact stated directly.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Fixing grammar and punctuation
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Correct five common kinds of grammar and punctuation mistakes in sentences.
This lesson builds toward: Given sentences with errors, you will correct mistakes in grammar, punctuation, capitalization and word choice, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Many RLA questions show a sentence with a drop-down choice and ask which version is correct. A few mistakes come up again and again. Learn these and you will get many points.
1) Subject and verb agree: "The list of jobs is long" (the subject is list, not jobs). 2) Complete sentences: "Because the bus was late." is a fragment; fix it: "I was late because the bus was late." 3) Run-ons: "I applied I got the job" needs a period, a semicolon or a joining word: "I applied, and I got the job."
4) Words that sound alike: their (belongs to them), there (a place), they're (they are); its (belongs to it), it's (it is); your (belongs to you), you're (you are). 5) Capital letters and apostrophes: names of people, places and days take capitals (Monday, Texas); an apostrophe shows ownership (the manager's office) or a missing letter (don't), not a plural (two shifts, not two shift's).
Transition words link ideas: however (but), therefore (so), for example, in addition. Pick the one that fits the meaning between the two sentences.
Step by step:
- Read the whole sentence, not just the underlined part.
- Find the subject and the verb, and check they agree.
- Check it is a complete sentence and not two sentences run together.
- Check sound-alike words, capitals and apostrophes.
- Read the choice you picked back in the sentence to be sure it sounds right.
Words to know:
- Subject: who or what the sentence is about.
- Verb: the action or being word, like runs or is.
- Fragment: a piece of a sentence that cannot stand alone.
- Run-on: two sentences joined with no correct punctuation.
- Transition: a word that links two ideas, like however or therefore.
Try it now: Fix each sentence. 1) "The box of gloves are on the shelf." 2) "Their going to the job fair on friday." 3) "I finished my shift I went home." 4) "The company changed it's hours." 5) "Because I wanted to learn." Answers: 1) "is" (the subject is box). 2) "They're going to the job fair on Friday." 3) "I finished my shift, and I went home." 4) "its" (belongs to it). 5) Add a main idea: "I signed up for class because I wanted to learn."
You can now spot and fix the most common grammar and punctuation mistakes on the test.

options: The team of nurses are ready.
The team of nurses were ready.
The team of nurses is ready.
The team of nurses be ready.
check.why: The subject is team (one group), so the verb is is.

check.q: Which word fits: "___ going to start training on Monday."
check.why: They're means they are: they are going to start training.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Arguments and the extended response

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Claims, evidence and strong reasons
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the claim and the evidence in an argument and rate each piece of evidence as strong or weak.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short argument, you will identify the claim and the evidence and rate each piece of evidence as strong or weak, giving a reason for each rating.
An argument tries to convince you. The claim is what the writer wants you to believe. The evidence is what they use to prove it.
Strong evidence is specific and can be checked: numbers from a study or a record, facts, or an expert in that field. Weak evidence is a feeling, one person's story used to stand for everyone, a famous person who is not an expert, or a claim with no proof.
Worked example. Claim: "Our town should add a bus route to the industrial park." Evidence A: "A county survey of 600 workers found 1 in 4 miss shifts because of rides." Strong: a number from a survey. Evidence B: "My cousin says the bus would be nice." Weak: one person's opinion.
Also watch for tricks: words like "everyone knows", attacks on a person instead of their idea, and only two choices when there are more.
Step by step:
- Find the claim: what does the writer want you to believe?
- Underline each piece of evidence.
- Ask: is it specific, and could I check it?
- Rate it strong or weak, and write one reason why.
Words to know:
- Argument: writing that tries to convince you of something.
- Claim: the main point a writer wants you to believe.
- Strong evidence: specific facts or numbers you could check, or an expert in that field.
- Weak evidence: feelings, one story, or claims with no proof.
Try it now: Practice argument: "The city should plant more trees downtown. A city study measured streets with trees at about 10 degrees cooler in summer. A local singer said trees look nice. Anyone who disagrees just hates nature." Find the claim and rate each piece of support. Answers: Claim: plant more trees downtown. City study: strong (a measured number from a study). Singer: weak (not an expert; just an opinion). "Anyone who disagrees hates nature": weak (attacks people instead of giving proof).
You can now find the claim, sort strong evidence from weak, and say why.

check.q: Which is the strongest evidence that a job training program works?
options: The director says it is great
Records show 70% of graduates found jobs within six months
check.why: It is a specific number from records that could be checked.

check.q: "My neighbor got sick after eating there, so the restaurant is unsafe." What kind of evidence is this?
check.why: One story does not prove something about every meal there.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Comparing two arguments and planning your essay
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare two arguments and write a short plan for an extended response.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short argument, you will identify the claim and the evidence and rate each piece of evidence as strong or weak, giving a reason for each rating. Given two passages that disagree, with a 45-minute timer, you will write an extended response that picks the better-supported argument and explains why with evidence, with an introduction, at least two pieces of evidence from the passages and a conclusion.
On the test you read two passages that take different sides. Ged.com says you analyze them, decide which argument has more convincing evidence, and explain why. You are not asked which side you agree with; you judge the evidence.
Use a simple chart. For each passage, write the claim, the evidence, and a mark for strong or weak. The passage with more strong evidence is usually your pick, even if you personally believe the other side.
Spend about 10 minutes planning. Your plan: 1) your thesis, one sentence that says which argument is better supported; 2) two or three pieces of evidence from that passage and why they are strong; 3) one weakness in the other passage.
Practice passages are in Lesson 6. Today, practice the chart with any two short opinion articles that disagree, such as two letters to the editor.
Step by step:
- Read both passages and find each claim.
- Make a two-column chart: evidence in each passage.
- Mark each piece of evidence strong or weak.
- Write one thesis sentence: which argument is better supported.
- List the evidence you will use in each body paragraph.
Words to know:
- Thesis: one sentence that states your main point; in the GED essay, which argument is better supported.
- Analyze: look closely at the parts to see how they work.
- Body paragraph: a middle paragraph that gives one reason with evidence.
Official sources:
- GED Testing Service: Reasoning Through Language Arts
Try it now: Practice: Passage 1 says a four-day work week is good and cites a company record: sick days fell from 6 to 4 per worker in a year. Passage 2 says it is bad because "workers will get lazy" and a manager "has a feeling" output will drop. Write a thesis. Answer: "Passage 1 is better supported because it uses company records on sick days, while Passage 2 relies on feelings with no data."
You can now compare two arguments with a chart and write a thesis and plan for your essay.

check.q: What does the GED extended response ask you to do?
options: Write about your own life story
Decide which argument has more convincing evidence and explain why
check.why: Ged.com says you analyze two passages and explain which argument has better evidence.

check.q: You agree with Passage B, but Passage A has more strong evidence. Which should your thesis pick?
options: Passage A, because it is better supported
Passage B, because you agree with it
check.why: The essay judges the evidence, not your opinion on the topic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing the extended response in 45 minutes
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a timed extended response that picks the better-supported argument and explains why with evidence.
This lesson builds toward: Given two passages that disagree, with a 45-minute timer, you will write an extended response that picks the better-supported argument and explains why with evidence, with an introduction, at least two pieces of evidence from the passages and a conclusion.
Use a simple shape. Introduction (2 to 3 sentences): name the topic and give your thesis. Body paragraphs (two or three): each gives one reason, quotes or describes evidence from the passage, and explains why it is strong or weak. Conclusion (2 sentences): restate your thesis in new words.
Practice passages (made up for this course). Passage A, by the city librarian: "Keep the main library open until 9 pm. During a three-month trial, our door counter recorded about 340 visits after 6 pm each week. Our computer log shows that 6 in 10 job-search sessions happened after 6 pm. The extra hours cost less than 1% of our budget." Passage B, by a council member: "Close at 6 pm. I walked by one evening and it looked empty. People can just use their phones. It is a waste of money."
Time plan: about 10 minutes to read and plan, 30 minutes to write, 5 minutes to proofread. Use transition words (first, in addition, however, therefore). Write in complete sentences and your own words, and quote short pieces of the passages as evidence.
Proofread for the mistakes from Lesson 3: subject and verb, run-ons, sound-alike words, capitals and apostrophes.
Step by step:
- Set a 45-minute timer.
- Read both passages and fill in your strong-or-weak chart (about 10 minutes).
- Write the introduction with your thesis.
- Write two or three body paragraphs, each with evidence and why it is strong or weak.
- Write a short conclusion.
- Proofread in the last 5 minutes.
Words to know:
- Introduction: the first paragraph; it names the topic and gives your thesis.
- Conclusion: the last paragraph; it restates your main point.
- Quote: copy a few exact words from the passage, inside quotation marks.
- Proofread: read your writing again to find and fix mistakes.
Try it now: Final task: set a 45-minute timer and write your extended response on the library passages above. Then proofread and score it with the rubric. Model thesis: "Passage A is better supported because it uses the library's own visit counts and computer records, while Passage B relies on one evening's look and opinions." Strong evidence to use: about 340 visits after 6 pm each week; 6 in 10 job-search sessions after 6 pm; cost under 1% of the budget. Weakness in B: one visit, no numbers.
You can now write a complete, timed extended response that judges two arguments by their evidence.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear thesis No thesis, or it says which side the writer agrees with instead of which is better supported. The introduction has one sentence that says which argument is better supported. The thesis also names the main reason, such as records versus opinions. Evidence from the passages No evidence from the passages, or evidence is made up. At least two pieces of evidence from the passages, each explained as strong or weak. Also points out a trick or weakness in the other passage and explains it. Organization One block of text, or ideas jump around. Introduction, at least two body paragraphs and a conclusion, with transition words. Each body paragraph opens with a clear topic sentence that ties back to the thesis. Grammar and punctuation Many errors make it hard to read. A few small errors, but the meaning is always clear. Almost no errors; sound-alike words, capitals and apostrophes are all correct. Reading accuracy Gets the main idea of a passage wrong. Describes each passage's main idea correctly. Uses short exact quotes that match what the passages say. Plan and timing Did not finish in 45 minutes and has no study plan. Finished in 45 minutes and the study plan has dates through test week. Also booked a GED Ready practice test or a real test date on ged.com. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, practice that part and write a new essay on a new pair of passages.

check.why: The introduction names the topic and states which argument is better supported.

check.q: In the library passages, which is the strongest evidence?
options: The door counter recorded about 340 visits after 6 pm each week
check.why: It is a specific number from a record that could be checked.
